newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Harnischfeger's Beloit needs change.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Harnischfeger's Beloit needs change.

text.p: Beloit Corp "isn't broken", but its performance does not meet Harnischfeger Industries Inc's expectations, Harnischfeger chief executive Jeffery T. Grade told Reuters.
But even without the restructuring announced last week, Beloit's five year outlook is "fairly impressive," Grade said.
The subsidiary "has to change in several key ways to be as profitable...as we want," he said about changes being made at the sole North American producer of pulp and paper machinery and systems.
The Beloit restructuring emphasizes service for all paper making equipment rather than focusing on equipment sales.
Grade said this is being done with the expectation that customers will come to the support provider first when they need new equipment.
"The after market is twice (the size) of the original equipment market," he added.
To accommodate this market, Beloit will hire engineers to staff service centers it is establishing.

The centers will be within one day's travel of sites where the company's paper making equipment is in use and Beloit will have one team to each customer instead of the up 18 individuals or groups that served each customer in the past.
The restructuring will result in a pretax charge of $50 million and spokesman David Brukardt said this will cut fourth quarter earnings by between $0.65 and $0.70 per share.

Grade declined to comment on results for the quarter, which ended on Thursday, but he did note that analysts had adjusted estimates down after the company's mid-September warning that earnings could be about 10 percent below projections. The First Call consensus estimate, excluding the charge, is now $0.84 per share.

Grade said most of the charge involves severance costs as the restructuring would reduce Beloit's worldwide staff by about 500. But nearly as many would be hired because the subsidiary's employment levels will be little changed.
The layoffs will take place at Beloit's manufacturing facilities, each of which now produces the full range of the company's product line.
By specializing at each plant, Beloit hopes to cut costs 30 percent, while building machines 30 percent faster. The changes will also increase manufacturing capacity 25 percent.
With the changes at Beloit, Harnischfeger is seeking to "repeat a success formula," Grade said.
A similar restructuring was made by Joy Manufacturing in 1990 and adopted for all of Harnischfeger's mining equipment operations after it acquired Joy in 1994, he added.
